ἀνθρώπων ὀνομάζεσθαι αὐτούς, ἀπ' αὐτῆς τῆς ἀρχῆς τῶν ἀγώνων τοῦ ὀνόματος
Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μέμνηται, ἀφ' οὗ προσήκει πάντας καλεῖσθαι. οὐ περὶ δογμάτων δὲ τὸ
νῦν λεγόμενον, οὐδὲ περὶ τούτου μέμφεται αὐτοῖς, ἀλλὰ περὶ οὗ προείπομεν καὶ τὰ
ἑξῆς δείκνυσιν. 1 Kor 1,13. 17α Μὴ συγκληρονόμους, φησίν, ἔχει Χριστὸς μεθ' ὧν
ἐμερίσατο ὑμᾶς πιστεύοντας; οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν «ἐμερίσθη Χριστός;» ἀλλὰ μὴ ἐμερίσατο
Χριστὸς μεθ' ὑμῶν; καὶ τοῦτο ἡ ἐπαγωγὴ δείκνυσιν· λέγει γάρ· μὴ Παῦλος
ἐσταυρώθη ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν; ὁ ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου σωτηρίας ἀποθανὼν Χριστός, ἡμῶν
δὲ οὐδείς.Ἀπὸ τούτου δείκνυσιν ὅτι τινὲς ἀπὸ τοῦ βαπτίσαντος αὐτοὺς ὀνομάζεσθαι
ἐβούλοντο. τοῦτο τὸ καλὸν ὃ καὶ προσέταξεν ὁ σωτήρ, καὶ σωτηρίαν φέρει, ἐμοί,
φησί, βάρος ἐγίνετο, εἰ ἐμέλλετε ἀπ' ἐμοῦ τοῦ βαπτίσαντος καλεῖσθαι. πῶς δὲ
νοήσομεν τὸ οὐκ ἀπέστειλέν με Χριστὸς βαπτίζειν ἀλλ' εὐαγγελίζεσθαι; ἐπεὶ
βαπτίζει μὲν καὶ ὁ μὴ ἀπόστολος, τὸ δὲ τῆς ἀποστολῆς ἀξίωμα εἶχον ὀλίγοι, καὶ ἄνευ
τοῦ εὐαγγελισθῆναι καὶ βαπτισθῆναι οὐκ ἐνῆν βαπτισθῆναι, φησίν· εὐαγγελίσασθαι
ἀπεστάλην· τοῦτο γὰρ τὸ προηγούμενον, οὐ τὸ βαπτίσαι. λείπει οὖν ἐνταῦθα τὸ
προηγουμένως οὐκ ἀπεστάλην βαπτίσαι. οὕτως καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ ὅταν λέγῃ· μὴ τῶν
βοῶν μέλει τῷ θεῷ; οὐκ ἐπειδὴ οὐ μέλει· καὶ γὰρ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ περὶ βοῶν λέγει
Μωϋσῆς, ἀληθῶς περὶ τῶν ὑπηρετουμένων τοῖς γεωργοῖς. φησὶ δὲ καὶ ὁ ∆αυίδ·
ἀνθρώπους καὶ κτήνη σώσεις κύριε, ὡς ἐπλήθυνας τὸ ἔλεός σου ὁ θεός. λέγει δὲ καὶ
Σολομῶν· οἰκτείρει δίκαιος ψυχὰς κτηνῶν αὐτοῦ, πόσῳ δὲ μᾶλλον ὁ θεός; ἀλλ' ὅ
φησιν, τί ἐστιν; ὅτι προηγουμένως τῶν βοῶν οὐ μέλει τῷ θεῷ. καὶ ἐνταῦθα κατ'
ἔλλειψιν ὡς καὶ τὸ οὐκ ἀπέστειλέν με Χριστὸς βαπτίζειν. 228 1 Kor 1,17 Μεταβαίνων
ἐφ' ἕτερον ἔγκλημα καὶ ἐπ' ἄλλην διόρθωσιν ἐρχόμενος, οὐκ ἀποθέμενος τέλεον τὸ
πρῶτον, προοιμίῳ κέχρηται τῷ δευτέρῳ· τὸ μὲν γὰρ οὐκ ἀπέστειλέν με Χριστὸς
βαπτίζειν τοῦ πρώτου ἐγκλήματος ἦν, τοῦ ὅτι ἕκαστος ὑμῶν λέγει· ἐγὼ μέν εἰμι
Παύλου, ἐγὼ δὲἈπολλώ, τὸ δὲ οὐκ ἐν σοφίᾳ λόγον ἀρχῆς ἑτέρας οἰκονομίας.
τέθεικεν οὖν τὸ εὐαγγελίζεσθαι τέλος μὲν τοῦ πρώτου πράγματος, ἀρχὴν δὲ τοῦ
δευτέρου. Ἵνα μὴ κενωθῇ ὁ σταυρὸς τοῦ Χριστοῦ. ἐὰν γὰρ τῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων
συνέσει καὶ τῇ παιδεύσει τὸ κήρυγμα ἐπιγράφηται, ἡ δύναμις τοῦ σταυροῦ οὐ
δείκνυται. 1 Kor 1,18–20 Ὁ λόγος ὁ τοῦ σταυροῦ. οὐ τὸ ῥῆμα λέγει οὐδὲ τὴν
προφοράν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δύναμιν· τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἔργον ἀσθενὲς εἶναι φαίνεται, ἡ δὲ αἰτία
ζητουμένη μέγα μυστήριον δείκνυται. Τοῖς δὲ σωζομένοις ἡμῖν δύναμις θεοῦ ἐστιν.
ἐπειδὴ τὸ Χριστὸς θεοῦ δύναμις καὶ θεοῦ σοφία εἰς τὸν θεοῦ λόγον λαμβάνειν τινὲς
βούλονται, ἐντεῦθεν παρατηρητέον ὅτι δύναμιν θεοῦ λέγει τοῦ σταυροῦ τὸν λόγον.
Γέγραπται γάρ· ἀπολῶ τὴν σοφίαν τῶν σοφῶν. εἰ καὶ ἀξιόπιστος καθ' ἑαυτὸν
διδάσκων ὁ ἀπόστολος–Χριστὸν γὰρ εἶχεν ἐν ἑαυτῷ λαλοῦντα–ἀλλ' οὖν κέχρηται
καὶ τῇ μαρτυρίᾳ τῆς παλαιᾶς διαθήκης, ἰσχυροτέραν τὴν πληροφορίαν ἐργαζόμενος
τῶν μαθητῶν. χρησάμενος δὲ τῇ μαρτυρίᾳ τῇ ἀπολῶ τὴν σοφίαν τῶν σοφῶν, λοιπὸν
ὡς ἐφ' ὡμολογημένοις ἐπεξέρχεται λέγων· ποῦ σοφός; ποῦ γραμματεύς;
σοφὸςἙλλήνων, γραμματεὺς δὲ τῶνἸουδαίων. 1 Kor 1,21 ∆ύο σοφιῶν μέμνηται·
μίας τῆς ἐν τοῖς δημιουργήμασι θεωρουμένης ἁρμονίας, ἑτέρας δὲ σοφίας καθ' ἣν
λογικοὶ ὄντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι συνετοὶ τυγχάνοντες. ἐπειδὴ τοίνυν, φησί, διὰ τῆς
προσούσης ἡμῖν συνέσεως οὐκ ἔγνωμεν τὸν θεόν, οὔτε διὰ τῆς ἐν τοῖς
δημιουργήμασι θεωρουμένης σοφίας, εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς διὰ τῆς μωρίας τοῦ
κηρύγματος σῶσαι τοὺς πιστεύοντας. μέγα ἐστὶν ὃ λέγει, οὐ δεικνυόμενον τοῖς
ἁπλῶς παρατρέχουσιν· τὸ γὰρ δυνατὸν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πάνσοφον δείκνυσιν οὕτως. τὸ
μέγεθος καὶ τὸ κάλλος τοῦ κόσμου, φησίν, ἀμέτρητον ὂν καὶ ἀνέφικτον, οὐκ ἔπεισεν
ὑμᾶς ἐπιγνῶναι 229 τὸν θεόν, ἀλλ' ἀφέντες τὸν ποιήσαντα προσεκυνήσατε τούτοις
δι' ὧν ἐχρῆν ἐπιγνῶναι τὸν ποιητὴν αὐτῶν. δεικνὺς ὑμῖν ὁ θεὸς τῆς ἑαυτοῦ
δυνάμεως τὴν ὑπερβολήν, οὓς οὐκ ἔπεισε κτίσις ἀλλὰ καὶ ἔπληξε, διὰ τῆς
ὁμολογουμένης ἀσθενείας τοῦ σταυροῦ κόσμον ἐφώτισεν. 1 Kor 1,22–25 ∆εικνὺς γὰρ
τὴν ἀτοπίαν τῶν ἐν λογιότητι τεθαρσηκότων καὶ κοσμεῖν οἰομένων διὰ τῆς
εὐγλωττίας τὴν εὐσέβειαν, φησὶν ὅτι οὐ μόνον σοφίαν τοῖςἝλλησι ζητοῦσιν οὐ χρὴ
ἀποκρίνεσθαι, ἀλλ' οὐδὲ σημεῖα αἰτοῦσι τοῖςἸουδαίοις διδόναι. καὶ μὴν τὰ σημεῖα
τοῦ πνεύματος, ἡ δὲ σοφία τῶν λόγων τῆς ἔξωθεν παιδείας. εἰ δὲ οὐδὲ τὰ τοῦ
πνεύματος θαύματα αἰτοῦσι προσῆκεν ἤπου τε τὰ τῆς ἔξωθεν σοφίας– οὐ γὰρ
pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: so as to persuade them not from) men to be named, from the very beginning of the contests he mentions the name of Jesus Christ, from whom it is fitting that all be called. What is now said is not about doctrines, nor does he blame them about this, but about what we said before, and the following things show (it). [Label 1 Cor 1:13, 17a.] Does Christ, he says, have co-heirs, with whom he divided you who believe? For he did not say 'Was Christ divided?' but 'Did Christ divide (it) with you?' And the following (words) show this: for he says, 'Was Paul crucified for us?' The one who died for the salvation of the world is Christ, and none of us. From this he shows that some wanted to be named from the one who baptized them. This good thing, which the Saviour commanded and which brings salvation, became a burden to me, he says, if you were going to be called from me who baptized. How shall we understand 'Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel'? Since one who is not an apostle also baptizes, but few had the dignity of apostleship, and without being evangelized (and being baptized - apparently repeated by a copying slip) it was not possible to be baptized, he says: I was sent to evangelize; for this is the leading thing, not baptizing. So there is lacking here the (word) 'primarily': I was not sent primarily to baptize. So also elsewhere when he says 'Is it for oxen that God cares?' (1 Cor 9:9): not because he does not care; for in the law Moses speaks about oxen, truly about those that serve the farmers. And David says: 'Men and beasts you will save, Lord, as you multiplied your mercy, O God' (Ps 35:7-8 LXX = 36:6-7). And Solomon says: 'A righteous man pities the souls of his beasts' (Prov 12:10) - how much more God? But what he says, what is it? That primarily God does not care for oxen. And here (it is) by ellipsis, as also 'Christ did not send me to baptize'. [Label 1 Cor 1:17.] Passing to another charge and coming to another correction, not having set aside the first completely, he has used (it) as preface for the second. For 'Christ did not send me to baptize' was of the first charge, that each of you says 'I am of Paul, I of Apollos'; but 'not in wisdom of word' (is) of the beginning of another arrangement. So he placed 'to evangelize' as the end of the first matter and the beginning of the second. 'Lest the cross of Christ be emptied.' For if the preaching is ascribed to the intelligence and education of men, the power of the cross is not shown. [Label 1 Cor 1:18-20.] 'The word of the cross.' He does not mean the phrase nor the utterance, but the power; for the deed appears to be weak, but the cause, when sought, is shown (to be) a great mystery. 'But to us who are saved it is the power of God.' Since some want to take 'Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God' to (refer to) God the Word, from here one must observe that he calls the word of the cross the power of God. 'For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise' (Isa 29:14). Even though the apostle was trustworthy teaching by himself - for he had Christ speaking in him (2 Cor 13:3) - yet he uses also the testimony of the Old Covenant, making the full assurance of the disciples stronger. Having used the testimony 'I will destroy the wisdom of the wise', he then proceeds as on agreed (ground), saying 'Where is the wise? Where is the scribe?' - wise (man) of the Greeks, scribe of the Jews. [Label 1 Cor 1:21.] He mentions two wisdoms: one, the harmony observed in the created works; another, the wisdom according to which humans, being rational, happen to be intelligent. Since then, he says, through the understanding present in us we did not know God, nor through the wisdom observed in the created works, God was pleased through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe. Great is what he says, not shown to those who simply run past; for thus he shows the power and all-wisdom of God. The greatness and the beauty of the world, he says, being measureless and unreachable, did not persuade you to know God, but leaving the one who made (them) you worshipped these, through which you ought to have known their maker. God, showing you the excess of his own power, through the confessed weakness of the cross enlightened the world - those whom creation did not persuade but even struck (with awe). [Label 1 Cor 1:22-25.] For showing the absurdity of those who were confident in learning and thought to adorn godliness through eloquence, he says that not only must one not answer the Greeks seeking wisdom, but not even give signs to the Jews asking. And yet the signs (are) of the Spirit, but the wisdom of words of the outside education. If it was not fitting (to give) even the wonders of the Spirit to those asking, surely (not) the things of outside wisdom - for not (… continues in the next section).
pass_b_english: …men, he recalls the name of Jesus Christ, after whom everyone ought to be called, from the very start of the contest. What he says now is not about doctrines, and he does not blame them for that, but for what we mentioned before, as the words that follow show.

On 1 Corinthians 1:13 and 1:17a: Does Christ have co-heirs, he asks, with whom he has shared you out, you who believe? He did not say, "Was Christ divided?" but, "Did Christ share out with you?" The words that follow show this, for he says, "Was Paul crucified for us?" Christ died for the salvation of the world; none of us did. From this he shows that some wanted to be named after the man who baptized them. This good thing, he says, which the Savior commanded and which brings salvation, would have become a burden to me if you were going to be called after me because I baptized you. How then shall we understand "Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel"? Someone who is not an apostle can baptize, while few held the rank of apostle, and no one could be baptized without first hearing the gospel. So he says, "I was sent to preach the gospel": that is the chief thing, not baptizing. The word "chiefly" is left out here: I was not sent chiefly to baptize. He speaks the same way elsewhere, when he says, "Is it for oxen that God cares?" (1 Corinthians 9:9). That is not because God does not care for them. In the law Moses really does speak about oxen, the beasts that serve farmers. David too says, "Men and beasts you will save, O Lord, as you have multiplied your mercy, O God" (Psalm 36:6–7). And Solomon says, "The righteous man pities the lives of his beasts" (Proverbs 12:10); how much more God? What then does he mean? That God does not care chiefly for oxen. Here too the sense is elliptical, just like "Christ did not send me to baptize."

On 1 Corinthians 1:17: As he moves on to another charge and comes to another correction, without wholly laying the first aside, he makes the end of the first serve as the opening of the second. "Christ did not send me to baptize" belonged to the first charge, that each of you says, "I am of Paul," and "I am of Apollos." But "not in wisdom of speech" begins a different line of treatment. So he set "to preach the gospel" as both the end of the first matter and the beginning of the second. "So that the cross of Christ may not be emptied": if the preaching is credited to human intelligence and learning, the power of the cross is not shown.

On 1 Corinthians 1:18–20: "The word of the cross." He does not mean the spoken phrase or its utterance, but its power. The deed looks weak, but when you look for its cause, it proves to be a great mystery. "But to us who are being saved it is the power of God." Some want to take "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" as said of God the Word; so we should note here that he calls the word of the cross the power of God. "For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise" (Isaiah 29:14). The apostle could have been trusted when teaching on his own authority, since he had Christ speaking in him (2 Corinthians 13:3). Even so he also draws on the witness of the Old Testament, and so makes his disciples' conviction stronger. Having used the text "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise," he goes on as if the point were already granted: "Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe?" The wise man is the Greek's; the scribe is the Jews'.

On 1 Corinthians 1:21: He speaks of two wisdoms. One is the harmony seen in the things God made. The other is the wisdom by which human beings, being rational, have understanding. Since, he says, we did not know God through the understanding we have, nor through the wisdom seen in the things he made, God was pleased to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching. What he says is great, and it does not show itself to those who skim past it, for this is how he displays God's power and complete wisdom. The size and beauty of the world, he says, measureless and beyond reach as they are, did not persuade you to know God. Instead you left the Maker and worshiped the very things through which you should have come to know him. To show you the surpassing greatness of his power, God enlightened the world through the confessed weakness of the cross, enlightening people whom creation had not persuaded but only overawed.

On 1 Corinthians 1:22–25: He shows how absurd it is for people to rely on learning and to think that eloquence adorns godliness. One must not answer the Greeks who look for wisdom, he says; one must not even give signs to the Jews who ask for them. Yet signs belong to the Spirit, while wisdom of words belongs to outside learning. If it was not right to give even the wonders of the Spirit to those who asked, how much less the things of outside wisdom (for one is not…

choices.english: Did Christ share out with you?
choices.why: Severianus reads the verb as middle (Christ dividing an inheritance with co-heirs); kept as he reads it.
rejected: Are you not heirs with Christ (old English, invents a question)

choices.term: ἄνευ τοῦ εὐαγγελισθῆναι καὶ βαπτισθῆναι οὐκ ἐνῆν βαπτισθῆναι
choices.english: no one could be baptized without first hearing the gospel
choices.why: The middle καὶ βαπτισθῆναι makes the clause say nothing; it looks like a copying slip and is noted, not rendered.
rejected: without being evangelized and being baptized, one could not be baptized

choices.why: Adverb of rank, not time; the old English 'previously' reversed the argument about oxen.
Greek Psalm numbering converted to English numbering; the quotation joins the end of 36:6 to 36:7.

choices.english: how much more God? (outside the quotation)
choices.why: Not part of Proverbs 12:10; Severianus' own inference.
